clean_label <- function(x) {
  s <- as.character(x)
  s <- gsub("&", "and", s, fixed = TRUE)
  s <- gsub("\u2013", "-", s, fixed = TRUE)
  s <- gsub("\u2014", "-", s, fixed = TRUE)
  s <- gsub("\\\\", "", s)
  s
}

subregions <- summary_data$subregions

)

# Abstract

Between the terminal Pleistocene occupation of highland caves in 10000BC and the threshold of Inca imperial expansion in 1438AD, human numbers across the Central Andes multiplied 250-fold, rising from an estimated 28,8k inhabitants to 7,2M across six biophysical sub-regions spanning 2.230.562,2 km² in Peru, Ecuador and Bolivia. Early foraging bands anchored along Pacific upwelling shores, coastal Las Vegas estuaries and inter-Andean karst shelters reached 188,65k by 6000BC and 756k by 3000BC as cotton, gourds, maize and tubers entered cultivation alongside early civic mounds at Valdivia Real Alto, Caral-Supe and Áspero [@solis2001dating; @haas2004dating; @gorbahn2013middle]. Subsequent ceremonial integration under Chavín de Huántar and Paracas lifted the regional total to 1,86M by 1000BC and 3,17M at 0AD [@turner1999geological; @tantalean2016final]. During the first millennium AD, canal-irrigated coastal states under Moche, Nasca and Lima, raised-field engineering around Lake Titicaca under Tiwanaku and sierra provincial networks under Wari drove aggregate density to 2,85 inhabitants per km² by 1000AD [@huckleberry2003geoarchaeological; @isbell2016wari; @stanish2003evolution]. Following a severe eleventh-century Altiplano contraction that lowered total headcount slightly from 6,37M in 1000AD to 6,32M in 1100AD, Late Intermediate polities led by Chimor at Chan Chan, Chincha, the Chachapoyas cloud-forest confederations, Aymara señoríos and northern Ecuadorian chiefdoms restored sustained growth to 7,2M inhabitants in 1438AD [@topic2003chan; @marconetto2019fin; @nystrom2010chachapoya]. This chapter calibrates those demographic trajectories against radiocarbon chronologies, valley-floor carrying capacities and a geocoded gazetteer of `r viscount_fmt_number(n_sites, 0L)` pre-Columbian habitation centres.

# Background

## Verticality, Coastal Upwelling and the Archaic Baseline (10000BC to 3000BC)

The human geography of the pre-Columbian Central Andes rested upon an extreme juxtaposition of ecological zones packed within narrow longitudinal transects. Rising abruptly from the cold Humboldt Current along the Pacific littoral to snowline cordilleras above 5.000 m before plunging eastward into cloud-draped Montaña valleys and the upper Amazon basin, the Andean spine compressed marine fisheries, hyper-arid oasis deltas, temperate Quechua valleys, frost-prone Suni and Puna grasslands and humid tropical piedmont within a few days' march. Pre-Columbian communities converted that steepness into demographic resilience through vertical complementarity, exchanging marine protein, lowland cotton, maize and coca for highland tubers, freeze-dried camelid meat, obsidian and salt.

At our opening benchmark of 10000BC, deglaciating mountain valleys and Pacific headlands held sparse mobile foraging bands numbering roughly 28,8k across 2.230.562,2 km² (0,013 inhabitants per km²). Inside the Central Sierra, long-stratified cave shelters such as Guitarrero Cave in the Callejón de Huaylas (30 to 140 inhabitants across its early occupation) and Pikimachay in Ayacucho (50 to 195) document broad-spectrum deer, guanaco and plant-gathering camps established immediately after Pleistocene ice retreat, later joined by specialised vicuña-hunting stations on the Junín Puna such as Telarmachay from 7000BC (85 to 240 inhabitants). Along the Peruvian littoral, early Holocene groups settled coastal fog lomas and estuary rims: Huaca Prieta at the mouth of the Chicama Valley records continuous mound accumulation beginning by 8000BC, while Middle Archaic communities at Pernil Alto on the Rio Grande de Nazca experimented with early sedentism and bottle-gourd, bean and tuber horticulture under shifting mid-Holocene moisture regimes [@gorbahn2013middle].

Further north, along the Santa Elena peninsula and Guayas coast of Ecuador, early Holocene Las Vegas foragers exploited mangrove shellfish, estuarine fish and garden plots, laying the demographic foundation for ceramic village life. By 6000BC, Central Andean population had grown more than sixfold to 188,65k (0,085 inhabitants per km²), and by 4000BC it reached 478,1k as camelid domestication in the central and southern highlands and intensified shellfish-and-anchovy harvesting along the Peruvian desert coast anchored semi-sedentary hamlets.

## Norte Chico, Valdivia and the First Andean Monumental Centres (3000BC to 1200BC)

During the third millennium BC, two distinct coastal hearths crossed into monumental village and proto-urban life well before pottery or metallurgy spread uniformly across the continent. In coastal Ecuador, the Las Vegas foraging tradition gave way around 3500BC to Valdivia ceramic farming villages centred on the Chanduy and Valdivia valleys. Real Alto, rising from 3200BC to a peak around 1.480 inhabitants by 2400BC, arranged elliptical wattle-and-daub dwellings around a central plaza flanked by paired ceremonial mounds, supported by maize, manioc and coastal fishing alongside sister settlements such as Loma Alta (peak 890 inhabitants at 2200BC). Simultaneously, along the eastern Andean foothills of Zamora-Chinchipe, the Mayo-Chinchipe community at Santa Ana-La Florida (established by 3300BC and reaching 1.120 inhabitants by 1500BC) built sunken circular stone plazas and traded cacao and marine Spondylus shell across the cordillera.

Further south along Peru's arid Norte Chico littoral, Late Archaic (Preceramic) societies achieved monumental urban scale between 3000BC and 1800BC without fired pottery. Anchored by irrigated cotton fields used for fishing nets and abundant Pacific anchovies harvested at coastal ports such as Áspero (peak 1.380 inhabitants at 2400BC) and Bandurria (960 at 2400BC), inland valley-floor centres constructed terraced platform pyramids and sunken circular courts aligned to solar and topographic sightlines [@solis2001dating; @haas2004dating; @gonzalezgarcia2021river]. Caral in the Supe Valley grew from 1.450 inhabitants in 2600BC to 3.120 at 2200BC, coordinating labour across nearby centres while sister traditions built stone-chambered hearths at La Galgada in the Tablachaca gorge (1.140 at 1800BC) and Kotosh on the eastern Huánuco slope (founded by 2200BC, reaching 1.890 at 800BC). Toward the close of the second millennium BC, massive Initial Period U-shaped temple complexes multiplied along the central and north-central coasts, including El Paraíso in the Chillón Valley (2.340 at 1600BC), Pampa de las Llamas-Moxeke (2.640 at 1200BC) and Sechín Alto (3.860 at 1200BC) in Casma, and coastal Las Haldas (1.480 at 1400BC). Total Central Andean population expanded accordingly from 756k in 3000BC to 1,18M in 2000BC.

## The Chavín Horizon, Paracas and Regional Diversification (1200BC to 200AD)

Between 1200BC and 200BC, Initial Period coastal temple centres waned under recurring El Niño flood disruptions and tectonic shifts, while demographic and ideological gravity shifted toward highland-coast pilgrimage hubs and early irrigation states. Positioned at 3.180 m at the confluence of the Mosna and Huachecsa rivers, Chavín de Huántar commanded a natural pass linking the Pacific coast, the Callejón de Huaylas and the eastern Marañón slopes [@turner1999geological]. Growing from 1.250 inhabitants in 1000BC to 3.680 at 400BC, Chavín projected a shared feline-and-raptor iconography across northern Peru, linking valley centres such as Pacopampa (2.140 at 800BC), Kuntur Wasi (1.820 at 600BC), Caballo Muerto in Moche (2.150 at 1000BC), Garagay in the Rimac Valley (1.790 at 1000BC) and Cardal in Lurín (1.620 at 900BC). Late in this horizon, the solar observatory and fortified sanctuary of Chankillo in Casma (1.340 inhabitants at 200BC) marked rising inter-valley conflict along the north-central coast. Across the northern sierra and eastern slopes, regional ceremonial heterogeneity persisted into later periods as local shrines and deities remained anchored in mountain topography [@guerrero2020san].

On the arid South Coast, Paracas communities in the Ica, Pisco, Chincha and Palpa valleys built extensive sunken-court ceremonial platforms and elite necropolises famed for polychrome textiles. Cerro del Gentil in Chincha illustrates late Paracas ritual aggregation prior to the Topará transition around 200BC [@tantalean2016final], while major settlement clusters developed at Ánimas Altas in the Ica Valley (reaching 4.180 inhabitants at 100BC) and Paracas Arena Blanca (2.420 at 0AD). Settlement-pattern modelling in Palpa and Nasca shows Paracas groups favouring mid-valley foothills before descending onto lower alluvial terraces as Nasca irrigation expanded [@bilotti2025points].

Far to the south, the Titicaca-Poopó Altiplano completed its own shift to sedentary agro-pastoral villages anchored on quinoa, bitter potatoes, oca and llama herding [@browman2004tierras; @stanish2003evolution]. Formative village mounds of Wankarani south of Lake Poopó (1.140 inhabitants at 100BC) and Chiripa on the Taraco Peninsula (1.620 at 300BC) yielded by 400BC to the nucleated northern basin centre of Pukara, which rose to 6.480 inhabitants at 200AD. Meanwhile, on the upper Amazonian flanks of Ecuador, communities in the Upano Valley began erecting vast gridded complexes of earthen platforms connected by straight sunken roads, led by Kilamope Upano (founded by 500BC, peaking at 11.600 by 300AD) and Sangay Upano (founded by 400BC, peaking at 9.450 by 400AD). Driven by maize expansion, camelid pastoralism and multi-valley irrigation, total Central Andean population climbed from 1,86M in 1000BC to 3,17M at 0AD.

## Regional States of the Early Intermediate Period (200AD to 600AD)

The centuries between 200AD and 600AD saw the emergence of dense, urbanised valley-kingdoms across the desert coast and sierra, lifting total population from 3,84M in 200AD to 5,49M in 600AD. On Peru's North Coast, the Moche state unified irrigated valleys from Piura to Nepeña through gravity-fed canal networks mapped across shifting alluvial terraces [@huckleberry2003geoarchaeological]. At its southern capital, Huacas de Moche, monumental adobe platforms - the Huaca del Sol and Huaca de la Luna - framed a dense artisan and administrative city that grew from 4.850 inhabitants in 200AD to 18.600 by 600AD [@moralesgamarra2020arquitectura]. Flanking Moche centres flourished at Sipán in Lambayeque (5.260 at 600AD), El Brujo in Chicama (4.120 at 500AD) and Pañamarca in Nepeña (3.180 at 600AD).

Along the Central Coast, the Lima culture engineered multi-valley irrigation canals feeding urban adobe-brick complexes at Maranga in the Rimac delta (growing from 3.180 in 200AD to 13.200 by 1400AD), Cajamarquilla (rising from 4.120 in 400AD to 11.200 in 600AD and 14.800 at 800AD) and the oracle sanctuary of Pachacamac in Lurín (founded by 200AD and expanding continuously to 19.400 by 1400AD). In the adjacent northern highlands, Recuay agro-pastoral chiefdoms erected stone-walled compounds and multi-storey chullpa mausolea across the Callejón de Huaylas, anchored at Honcopampa (3.340 at 800AD), while northern highland confederations built monumental stone galleries at Marcahuamachuco (6.940 at 800AD) and Cajamarca Layzón (growing from 1.480 in 200BC to 8.240 by 1350AD).

On the South Coast, Nasca society combined monumental ceremonial pilgrimages at Cahuachi (growing from 2.460 at 0AD to 6.120 at 200AD before waning after 400AD) [@silverman2009cahuachi] with sprawling desert geoglyph networks in Palpa and Nasca [@bolanosbaldassari2022paisajes]. Radiocarbon and luminescence chronologies confirm rapid demographic adjustment in the southern Nasca drainages as communities constructed subterranean filtration galleries (*puquios*), settled nucleated residential towns such as Ventilla (4.680 at 300AD) and Los Molinos Palpa (2.860 at 300AD) and intensified camelid provisioning [@vaughn2014about; @eerkens2024long]. In the southern Titicaca Basin, Khonkho Wankane (3.420 at 500AD) and early Tiwanaku (4.200 at 200AD, 16.800 at 500AD) pioneered monumental sunken courts and raised-field drainage.

## Middle Horizon Polities and Late Intermediate Urbanism (600AD to 1438AD)

Between 600AD and 1000AD, two highland empires reshaped Andean demography from opposite poles. In the Ayacucho Basin, the Wari state transformed its capital Wari from 6.800 inhabitants in 500AD to 38.400 by 850AD, surrounded by elite mortuary and craft satellites such as Conchopata (6.840 at 700AD) [@isbell2016wari; @valdez2006practicas]. Rather than ruling by loose prestige alone, Wari erected orthogonal, cellular administrative compounds linked by paved sierra roads - notably Pikillacta near Cusco (9.400 at 800AD), Viracochapampa in Huamachuco (3.820 at 800AD), Azángaro near Wari (2.960 at 850AD) and Jincamocco in Sondondo (2.840 at 800AD) [@schreiber1992wari]. Far south in the Moquegua Valley, Wari established a fortified summit colony at Cerro Baúl (3.620 at 800AD), provisioning state feasts and chicha brewing directly adjacent to Tiwanaku agrarian enclaves at Omo Moquegua (5.120 at 800AD) and Chen Chen (4.460 at 800AD) [@nash2011fiestas]. Meanwhile, on the North Coast, late Moche society adapted to severe sixth-century El Niño mega-floods and dunes by relocating inland to Pampa Grande in Lambayeque (11.800 at 700AD) and Galindo in the Moche Valley (7.850 at 700AD), alongside ceremonial-funerary centres at San José de Moro (3.840 at 800AD).

Simultaneously, Tiwanaku grew on the southeastern Titicaca shore into a metropolitan capital of 34.200 inhabitants at 800AD, flanked by lacustrine satellite cities at Lukurmata (9.840 at 900AD) and Pajchiri (4.160 at 800AD) [@stanish2003evolution; @loza2008fiera]. Supported by vast expanses of heat-retaining raised agricultural fields (*suka kollus*) across the Koani and Tiwanaku pampas, Tiwanaku exported arsenical-and-tin bronze metallurgy [@lechtman2005metalurgia], llama caravan ritual paraphernalia [@llagostera2006contextualizacion] and highland migrants verified through strontium isotopes as far afield as San Pedro de Atacama [@knudson2007influencia].

Around 1000AD to 1100AD, prolonged Altiplano aridity recorded in Quelccaya ice cores undermined raised-field hydraulics, fracturing Tiwanaku urbanism and triggering a rare regional demographic contraction across the Titicaca-Poopó Altiplano from 1,41M in 800AD to 1,26M in 1100AD [@marconetto2019fin]. Out of that fragmentation emerged fortified hilltop *pukaras* and competing Aymara señoríos (Colla, Lupaqa and Pacajes), anchored by Chucuito (12.650 at 1430AD), Hatuncolla (10.850 at 1430AD), Pucara de Juli (6.840), Chuquiabo Pre-Inca (6.780), Paria Oruro (5.840), Cutimbo (4.620) and terraced Mollo towns such as Iskanwaya (4.120), while late pre-Inca irrigation terraces intensified south-central highland yields [@albeck2019produccion].

On the North Coast, Sicán (Lambayeque) lords built monumental pyramid complexes at Batán Grande (11.400 at 1000AD) and Túcume (14.200 at 1400AD) before falling to the expanding Chimú empire (Chimor). From its sprawling adobe capital Chan Chan in the Moche Valley - rising from 8.400 inhabitants in 900AD to 42.500 by 1400AD across nine walled *ciudadelas* and artisan quarters [@topic2003chan] - Chimor integrated coastal valleys from Tumbes (Cabeza de Vaca, 6.180) and Piura (Narihualá, 7.480) through Jequetepeque (Farfán 6.920, Pacatnamú 7.140) south to Casma (Manchán, 4.860) and Paramonga (3.740). Further south, independent Late Intermediate polities prospered at Pachacamac (19.400), Armatambo (12.450) and Chancay Pisquillo (7.860) on the Central Coast, at La Centinela Chincha (18.900) and Chiribaya Alta (4.360) and Churajón (4.780) on the South Coast, and across terraced mountain ridges in the Central Sierra where Wanka cities at Tunanmarca (11.250) and Hatunmarca (8.740), Chanka centres at Sondor (7.120), Chachapoyas limestone citadels at Kuelap (4.920), Yalape (3.420) and Gran Pajatén (2.680) [@nystrom2010chachapoya], and Killke-phase Cusco (Qosqo Killke, 21.800 by 1430AD) stood poised on the eve of 1438AD. To the north, Caranqui mound chiefdoms (Quito Pre-Inca 14.800, Caranqui 9.120, Cochasquí 8.460, Zuleta 7.420), Puruhá and Cañari centres (Liribamba 7.180, Guapondelig 9.640, Hatun Cañar 8.920) and seafaring Manteño ports (Jocay 10.450, Agua Blanca 7.620, Peñón del Río 6.840, Salango 5.180) carried total Central Andean population to 7,2M by 1438AD.

# Methodology

## Biophysical Partition of the Six Sub-Regions

Because modern state boundaries cut arbitrarily across coastal desert valleys, high-altitude lake basins and Amazonian slopes, QUIPU divides the Central Andes across 2.230.562,2 km² into six coherent ecological and cultural sub-regions matching Figure 1:

1. North and Central Pacific Coast (Caral, Moche and Chimú), spanning 194.635,5 km² (8,7% of the study area) from Tumbes south past the Rimac and Lurín valleys to Chincha and the Callejón de Huaylas littoral fringe, capturing desert-oasis irrigation empires from Caral-Supe through Moche, Lima and Chimor.
2. South Coast and Atacama Valleys (Paracas, Nasca and Chincha), covering 85.213,6 km² (3,8%) across the hyper-arid Ica, Palpa, Nasca, Acarí and Arequipa coastal valleys.
3. Central Sierra (Chavín, Wari, Chanka and Early Cusco), encompassing 253.971 km² (11,4%) of inter-Andean basins from Chachapoyas and Cajamarca south through Ancash, Junín, Mantaro, Ayacucho, Andahuaylas and the Killke-phase Cusco heartland.
4. Titicaca-Poopó Altiplano (Tiwanaku and Aymara Señoríos), covering 529.905,1 km² (23,8%) across the high-altitude endorheic Titicaca and Poopó basins plus Moquegua and Arequipa western-slope enclaves.
5. Equatorial Sierra and Guayas (Cañari, Puruhá and Caranqui), spanning 181.000,1 km² (8,1%) across the Ecuadorian inter-Andean basins, Santa Elena, Guayas floodplains, Manabí coast and the upper Upano piedmont.
6. Eastern Montaña, Chachapoya and Yungas Slopes, encompassing 985.836,8 km² (44,2%) of humid cloud-forest foothills, Huánuco, Cochabamba, Mizque and Chuquisaca eastern valleys extending toward the Bolivian lowlands.

## Longitudinal Demographic Reconstruction and Carrying-Capacity Bounds

Pre-Columbian Andean polities left knot-recorded *khipu* censuses only after Inca imperial integration post-1438AD, and early Holocene societies left no written tallies at all. Sub-regional headcounts $P_r(t)$ across the 21 chronological benchmarks $t \in [-10000, 1438]$ are therefore reconstructed by coupling regional ecological carrying-capacity bounds with archaeological site-density trajectories, valley-floor canal-area estimates and calibrated radiocarbon activity [@solis2001dating; @bilotti2025points; @stanish2003evolution].

For each biophysical sub-region $r$ of terrestrial area $A_r$, population is expressed through its effective regional density $d_r(t)$:

$$P_r(t) = A_r \cdot d_r(t)$$

where $d_r(t)$ tracks the shift across successive subsistence regimes: from Late Pleistocene and Early Archaic hunting-gathering (0,01 to 0,09 inhabitants per km²) through Late Archaic and Formative incipient farming (0,2 to 0,9 inhabitants per km²) up to mature hydraulic irrigation and raised-field states (2,7 to 8,5 inhabitants per km²) [@gorbahn2013middle; @huckleberry2003geoarchaeological; @albeck2019produccion]. Between consecutive benchmarks $t_1$ and $t_2$, annualised compounding growth follows:

$$g_r(t_1, t_2) = \left(\frac{P_r(t_2)}{P_r(t_1)}\right)^{\frac{1}{t_2 - t_1}} - 1$$

Crucially, demographic momentum is never imposed monotonically where archaeological and palaeoclimatic evidence demonstrates contraction. In the Titicaca-Poopó Altiplano, the breakdown of raised-field agriculture during the eleventh-century drought is modelled explicitly as a negative growth interval between 800AD (1,41M) and 1100AD (1,26M) prior to demographic recovery under Late Intermediate Aymara señoríos [@marconetto2019fin; @stanish2003evolution].

## Gazetteer Assembly and Spatial Attribution

Alongside continuous sub-regional surfaces, QUIPU compiles an evidence-based gazetteer of `r viscount_fmt_number(n_sites, 0L)` geocoded habitation centres spanning Peru (78 sites), Ecuador (18) and Bolivia (13). Assembly proceeded through four documented ingestion waves logged in the chapter source ledger: Wave 1 harvested 68 centres from primary archaeological settlement-pattern surveys; Wave 2 integrated 27 sites from national heritage inventories including Peru's SIGDA Ministerio de Cultura register and Ecuador's INPC/CADB corpora; Wave 3 added 13 early Archaic and Formative radiocarbon anchors from Andean radiocarbon corpora; and Wave 4 verified 1 remaining sub-regional continuity site, reaching asymptotic saturation with a final marginal gain of 0,93% and zero reliance on crowd-sourced fallback entries (0%).

Individual settlement populations reflect excavated residential area, adobe or stone compound density, household counts and regional survey multipliers rather than uncalibrated monumental temple footprints [@isbell2016wari; @topic2003chan; @silverman2009cahuachi]. Where ceremonial pilgrimage sites such as Cahuachi or Chavín de Huántar supported smaller permanent resident populations alongside large seasonal gatherings, resident urban headcounts are scaled conservatively against residential terrace and domestic-refuse areas [@silverman2009cahuachi; @turner1999geological].

# Testing and Validation

## Cross-Checks Against Andean Palaeodemographic Benchmarks

To confirm that sub-regional totals align with archaeological survey realities and pre-1438AD agrarian carrying capacities, our estimates were cross-checked against four regional benchmarks. First, on the Peruvian North and Central Coast, valley-by-valley canal-command reconstructions for Moche, Lambayeque, Rimac-Lurín and Chincha indicate that Late Intermediate irrigated oases supported 1,4M to 1,9M inhabitants prior to Inca annexation [@huckleberry2003geoarchaeological; @topic2003chan]; our 1438AD estimate of 1,65M (8,48 inhabitants per km² across the broader coastal-desert polygon) sits squarely in the middle of that hydraulic envelope.

Second, in the Central Sierra, full-coverage regional pedestrian surveys in Ayacucho, Upper Mantaro, Andahuaylas and Cusco demonstrate high Late Intermediate *pueblo* nucleation, with Huari at 30k to 50k during the Middle Horizon and Killke-phase Cusco approaching 20k by the early fifteenth century [@isbell2016wari; @schreiber1992wari]; our estimates of 38,4k for Wari in 850AD, 21,8k for Qosqo Killke in 1430AD and 2,15M for the Central Sierra in 1438AD (8,47 inhabitants per km²) respect both site-level residential densities and regional arable terrace capacity.

Third, across the Titicaca-Poopó Altiplano, archaeological estimates for Tiwanaku's urban core plus peri-urban compounds range between 20k and 40k inhabitants at 800AD, sustained by up to 190 km² of mapped raised fields in the Pampa Koani and Katari valleys [@stanish2003evolution; @loza2008fiera]; our figures of 34,2k for Tiwanaku and 1,41M for the Altiplano in 800AD match those carrying-capacity calculations, while the 10,8% dip to 1,26M in 1100AD captures the documented post-collapse dispersal [@marconetto2019fin]. Fourth, in Ecuador, multi-temporal surveys along the Santa Elena coast, Upano piedmont and northern inter-Andean basins reconcile dense Late Integration chiefdoms (Quito Pre-Inca 14,8k, Jocay 10,45k, Guapondelig 9,64k) within a sub-regional total of 780k by 1438AD (4,31 inhabitants per km²).

## Sub-Regional Density Coherence and Growth Diagnostics

Table \ref{tab:subregion-benchmarks} summarises land area, population across six key chronological horizons (10000BC, 3000BC, 1000BC, 0AD, 800AD and 1438AD), final 1438AD density and catalogued site counts across all six sub-regions. Every sub-regional trajectory preserves ecological coherence, and the coastal and inter-Andean agrarian cores consistently sustain ten to fifteen times the areal density of the vast forested Eastern Montaña.

```{r tab-subregion-benchmarks, results='asis'}
rows <- lapply(subregions, function(r) {
  a <- as.numeric(r$area_km2)
  p1 <- as.numeric(r$population[["-10000"]])
  p2 <- as.numeric(r$population[["-3000"]])
  p3 <- as.numeric(r$population[["-1000"]])
  p4 <- as.numeric(r$population[["0"]])
  p5 <- as.numeric(r$population[["800"]])
  p6 <- as.numeric(r$population[["1438"]])
  d6 <- if (a > 0) p6 / a else 0
  sc <- summary_data$settlements_by_region[[r$id]]
  sc_val <- if (is.null(sc)) 0L else as.integer(sc)
  data.frame(
    Subregion = clean_label(r$name),
    Area = viscount_fmt_number(round(a), 0L),
    P10000 = viscount_fmt_pop(p1),
    P3000 = viscount_fmt_pop(p2),
    P1000 = viscount_fmt_pop(p3),
    P0 = viscount_fmt_pop(p4),
    P800 = viscount_fmt_pop(p5),
    P1438 = viscount_fmt_pop(p6),
    D1438 = viscount_fmt_number(d6, 2L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_bench <- do.call(rbind, rows)
df_tot <- data.frame(
  Subregion = "Central Andes Total",
  Area = viscount_fmt_number(round(tot_area), 0L),
  P10000 = viscount_fmt_pop(tot_10000),
  P3000 = viscount_fmt_pop(tot_3000),
  P1000 = viscount_fmt_pop(tot_1000),
  P0 = viscount_fmt_pop(tot_0),
  P800 = viscount_fmt_pop(tot_800),
  P1438 = viscount_fmt_pop(tot_1438),
  D1438 = viscount_fmt_number(tot_1438 / tot_area, 2L),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
df_bench <- rbind(df_bench, df_tot)
rownames(df_bench) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  df_bench,
  "Population headcounts and 1438AD densities (inhabitants per km²) across six Central Andean sub-regions from 10000BC to 1438AD.",
  c("Sub-Region", "Area (km²)", "10000BC", "3000BC", "1000BC", "0AD", "800AD", "1438AD", "1438AD Dens."),
  list(label = "tab:subregion-benchmarks", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

Over the entire 11.438-year interval from 10000BC to 1438AD, Central Andean population grew at a long-run compound annual rate of 0,048%, accelerating from 0,047% per annum across the Archaic and Formative millennia (10000BC to 0AD) to 0,084% per annum during the Early Intermediate and Middle Horizon urban surge (0AD to 800AD), before moderating to 0,023% per annum between 800AD and 1438AD as major coastal and highland valleys neared pre-Inca hydraulic saturation and the Altiplano weathered its eleventh-century downturn.

# Results

## Andean Demographic Trajectory (10000BC to 1438AD)

The Central Andean population curve displays a continuous S-shaped demographic transition marked by three distinct inflection regimes (Figure \ref{fig:central-andes-trajectory}). During the Archaic and Formative expansion from 10000BC to 1000BC, headcount climbed steadily from 28,8k to 1,86M as coastal shellfish-and-cotton sedentism merged with highland camelid herding and early maize cultivation [@gorbahn2013middle; @solis2001dating]. Between 1000BC and 800AD, state-scale irrigation canals, terrace systems and raised-field engineering propelled a rapid surge to 6,22M inhabitants. From 800AD to 1438AD, growth flattened into a mature plateau: aggregate headcount dipped briefly from 6,37M in 1000AD to 6,32M in 1100AD during Tiwanaku's collapse before recovering under Chimú, Chincha, Chanka and Killke-Cusco consolidation to reach 7,2M at 1438AD.

```{r fig-trajectory, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/pre_columbian_central_andes_population_trajectory.png",
  "Demographic trajectory for the Central Andes and leading sub-regions from 10000BC to 1438AD (Panel A) and sub-regional population density in 1438AD (Panel B).",
  "fig:central-andes-trajectory"
)
```

In 1438AD, demographic distribution remained sharply concentrated along the Andean spine and Pacific valleys. Despite holding just 23,9% of total land area, the Central Sierra (2,15M, 29,9% of total population), North and Central Pacific Coast (1,65M, 22,9%) and South Coast (620k, 8,6%) together accounted for 61,4% of all inhabitants. Including the Titicaca-Poopó Altiplano (1,45M, 20,1%) and Equatorial Sierra and Guayas (780k, 10,8%), five coastal and highland sub-regions occupying 55,8% of the land surface held 92,4% of the people, while the vast Eastern Montaña and Yungas slopes (44,2% of land area) held 7,6% (550k).

## Pacific Coast Valleys: Caral, Moche, Lima, Nasca and Chimor

The North and Central Pacific Coast (194.635,5 km²) sustained the highest final-benchmark density in the Central Andes at 8,48 inhabitants per km² in 1438AD (1,65M people), anchored by 44 catalogued settlements (2,26 sites per 10.000 km², the densest archaeological concentration in the chapter). From early coastal foundations at Huaca Prieta, Caral (3.120 at 2200BC), Áspero (1.380), Bandurria (960) and Sechín Alto (3.860 at 1200BC), population mounted from 173,25k in 3000BC to 726k at 0AD and 1,22M by 600AD as Moche and Lima engineers linked multi-valley river intakes [@haas2004dating; @huckleberry2003geoarchaeological]. Huacas de Moche reached 18.600 at 600AD [@moralesgamarra2020arquitectura], succeeded after El Niño shifts by Pampa Grande (11.800 at 700AD) and Galindo (7.850), while Sicán Batán Grande rose to 11.400 at 1000AD and Túcume to 14.200 at 1400AD. Under Chimor, Chan Chan peaked at 42.500 inhabitants in 1400AD [@topic2003chan], flanked down the coast by Cajamarquilla (14.800 at 800AD), Pachacamac (19.400 at 1400AD), Maranga (13.200), Armatambo (12.450) and the rich Chincha capital La Centinela (18.900).

South of Chincha, the hyper-arid South Coast and Atacama Valleys (85.213,6 km²) rose from 2,48k in 10000BC to 272,8k at 0AD, 517,7k in 800AD and 620k in 1438AD (7,28 inhabitants per km², third highest in the region). Here settlement hugged oasis river corridors and subterranean *puquio* aquifers, shifting from Paracas centres at Ánimas Altas (4.180) and Paracas Arena Blanca (2.420) to Nasca ceremonial and residential hubs at Cahuachi (6.120 at 200AD), Ventilla (4.680 at 300AD), Los Molinos Palpa (2.860) and La Muña (2.240), and Late Intermediate valleys such as Tambo Viejo (3.680) [@silverman2009cahuachi; @vaughn2014about; @bolanosbaldassari2022paisajes; @eerkens2024long].

## Central Sierra, Chachapoyas and Early Cusco

Holding 2,15M inhabitants across 253.971 km² in 1438AD (8,47 inhabitants per km², virtually tied with the North and Central Coast), the Central Sierra formed the demographic heartland of the Andean highlands. Growing from 8,6k in 10000BC to 225,75k in 3000BC and 559k in 1000BC during the Chavín horizon (Chavín de Huántar 3.680, Marcavalle near Cusco 1.640) [@turner1999geological], highland population surged to 946k at 0AD and 1,8M in 800AD under Wari urban expansion. Wari itself (38.400 at 850AD), Conchopata (6.840), Pikillacta (9.400) and Azángaro Wari (2.960) concentrated administrative, craft and mortuary populations along high-yield maize and tuber basins [@isbell2016wari; @schreiber1992wari; @valdez2006practicas].

During the Late Intermediate Period (1000AD to 1438AD), population dispersed upward onto defensible ridge towns while continuing to expand to 2,15M. In the Mantaro Valley, Wanka walled towns such as Tunanmarca (11.250 at 1430AD) and Hatunmarca (8.740) packed thousands of circular stone houses onto limestone crests. In Andahuaylas, Sondor Chanka reached 7.120, while across the northeastern cloud-forest escarpment, Chachapoyas settlements including Kuelap (4.920 at 1300AD), Yalape (3.420) and Gran Pajatén (2.680) coupled limestone ridge citadels with elaborate cliff-tomb mortuary landscapes [@nystrom2010chachapoya]. At the southern end of the corridor, Killke-phase Cusco (Qosqo Killke) grew steadily from 3.240 in 1000AD to 21.800 by 1430AD, forming the demographic launchpad of the Inca state.

## Titicaca-Poopó Altiplano: Pukara, Tiwanaku and the Aymara Señoríos

Spanning 529.905,1 km² above 3.800 m alongside western-slope Moquegua and Arequipa colonies, the Titicaca-Poopó Altiplano followed the region's only marked Middle Horizon reversal. Starting at 5,8k in 10000BC and reaching 369,75k in 1000BC through Wankarani (1.140) and Chiripa (1.620) agro-pastoral villages, population climbed through Pukara (6.480 at 200AD) and Khonkho Wankane (3.420 at 500AD) to a first peak of 1,41M in 800AD (2,67 inhabitants per km²) at the zenith of Tiwanaku (34.200), Lukurmata (9.840) and Pajchiri (4.160) [@stanish2003evolution; @browman2004tierras]. Long-distance Tiwanaku colonies and bronze-and-caravan exchange linked Omo Moquegua (5.120) and Chen Chen (4.460) to the Atacama oases [@nash2011fiestas; @lechtman2005metalurgia; @knudson2007influencia; @llagostera2006contextualizacion].

When eleventh-century drought collapsed raised-field surpluses, Altiplano population fell to 1,39M in 1000AD and 1,26M in 1100AD before pastoral and terraced farming rebounded under competing Lupaqa, Colla and Pacajes señoríos [@marconetto2019fin; @albeck2019produccion]. By 1438AD, fortified lakeside capitals at Chucuito (12.650), Hatuncolla (10.850), Pucara de Juli (6.840), Chuquiabo Pre-Inca (6.780), Paria Oruro (5.840) and Cutimbo (4.620), supported by coastal Chiribaya Alta (4.360) and Arequipa Churajón (4.780), restored regional headcount to 1,45M (2,74 inhabitants per km²).

## Equatorial Sierra, Guayas Littoral and the Upano Valley

Across 181.000,1 km² in Ecuador, population rose from 3,12k in 10000BC to 81,9k in 3000BC during the Valdivia florescence (Real Alto 1.480, Loma Alta 890), 343,2k at 0AD, 651,3k in 800AD and 780k in 1438AD (4,31 inhabitants per km²). Two ecological axes drove this growth: first, early piedmont urbanisation in the Upano Valley of the Ecuadorian Oriente, where Kilamope Upano (11.600 at 300AD) and Sangay Upano (9.450 at 400AD) thrived prior to volcanic ashfalls around 600AD; second, Late Integration chiefdoms across both the Guayas-Manabí littoral - where raised *camellones* at Peñón del Río (6.840) and Manteño maritime ports at Jocay (10.450), Agua Blanca (7.620) and Salango (5.180) traded *Spondylus* shell southward - and the inter-Andean basins, led by Quito Pre-Inca (14.800), Guapondelig (9.640), Caranqui (9.120), Hatun Cañar (8.920), Cochasquí (8.460), Zuleta (7.420), Liribamba Puruhá (7.180) and Tulipe (3.820).

## Eastern Montaña and Yungas Slopes

Although the Eastern Montaña, Chachapoya and Yungas Slopes cover 985.836,8 km² (44,2% of the chapter domain), steep forested relief, tropical soils and dispersed swidden-and-coca valleys kept density lowest at 0,56 inhabitants per km² in 1438AD (550k total, up from 2,2k in 10000BC and 242k at 0AD). Within fertile inter-montane basins along the Bolivian and Peruvian eastern escarpment, however, substantial towns developed at Cochabamba Pre-Inca (10.650 at 1430AD), Yotala Yampara (5.240), Mizque (4.680), Samaipata Pre-Inca (3.140) and Formative Kotosh (1.890 at 800BC).

## Pre-Inca Urban Hierarchy and Settlement Scaling

Across all `r viscount_fmt_number(n_sites, 0L)` catalogued pre-Columbian settlements, peak urban populations trace a steep yet coherent pre-imperial rank-size hierarchy (Figure \ref{fig:central-andes-hierarchy}). Fitting a power-law regression to the top rank tier yields $\alpha = 0,56$ ($R^2 = 0,98$), shallower than modern primate urban systems ($\alpha \approx 1$) because political power remained divided among competing valley kingdoms and sierra confederations rather than unified under one imperial metropolis prior to 1438AD.

```{r fig-hierarchy, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/pre_columbian_central_andes_urban_hierarchy.png",
  "Twelve largest recorded Central Andean settlements (Panel A) and settlement rank-size distribution across 109 catalogued sites (Panel B).",
  "fig:central-andes-hierarchy"
)
```

At the apex stood Chan Chan (42.500), Wari (38.400) and Tiwanaku (34.200), followed by Qosqo Killke (21.800), Pachacamac (19.400), La Centinela Chincha (18.900), Huacas de Moche (18.600), Cajamarquilla (14.800), Quito Pre-Inca (14.800), Túcume (14.200), Maranga (13.200) and Chucuito (12.650). Table \ref{tab:regional-shares} quantifies how each sub-region's share of total Central Andean population and areal density evolved from 10000BC through 1438AD alongside catalogued site recovery intensity.

```{r tab-regional-shares, results='asis'}
share_rows <- lapply(subregions, function(r) {
  a <- as.numeric(r$area_km2)
  p1 <- as.numeric(r$population[["-10000"]])
  p3 <- as.numeric(r$population[["-1000"]])
  p4 <- as.numeric(r$population[["0"]])
  p5 <- as.numeric(r$population[["800"]])
  p6 <- as.numeric(r$population[["1438"]])
  sh1 <- 100 * p1 / tot_10000
  sh4 <- 100 * p4 / tot_0
  sh5 <- 100 * p5 / tot_800
  sh6 <- 100 * p6 / tot_1438
  d4 <- if (a > 0) p4 / a else 0
  d6 <- if (a > 0) p6 / a else 0
  sc <- summary_data$settlements_by_region[[r$id]]
  sc_val <- if (is.null(sc)) 0L else as.integer(sc)
  site_dens <- if (a > 0) (sc_val / a) * 10000 else 0
  data.frame(
    Subregion = clean_label(r$name),
    Sh10 = paste0(viscount_fmt_number(sh1, 1L), "%"),
    Sh0 = paste0(viscount_fmt_number(sh4, 1L), "%"),
    Sh800 = paste0(viscount_fmt_number(sh5, 1L), "%"),
    Sh1438 = paste0(viscount_fmt_number(sh6, 1L), "%"),
    D0 = viscount_fmt_number(d4, 2L),
    D1438 = viscount_fmt_number(d6, 2L),
    SiteDens = viscount_fmt_number(site_dens, 2L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_shares <- do.call(rbind, share_rows)
rownames(df_shares) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  df_shares,
  "Sub-regional shares of Central Andean population, chronological densities (inhabitants per km²) and catalogued site recovery per 10.000 km², 10000BC to 1438AD.",
  c("Sub-Region", "10000BC %", "0AD %", "800AD %", "1438AD %", "0AD Dens.", "1438AD Dens.", "Sites/10k km²"),
  list(label = "tab:regional-shares", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

# Limitations

Four structural uncertainties govern demographic reconstruction across the pre-Columbian Central Andes. First, post-glacial marine transgression submerged early Pacific littoral camps from Santa Elena south to Ica between 10000BC and 4000BC, while river-delta alluviation and El Niño mega-floods buried Formative occupational strata along the North Coast and lower Guayas plain [@huckleberry2003geoarchaeological]. Terrestrial site counts consequently under-represent early maritime foraging populations relative to surviving upland caves and desert-margin mounds.

Second, archaeological survey intensity varies starkly across ecological zones. Coastal desert valleys in Peru enjoy exceptional surface preservation and long survey coverage (2,26 catalogued sites per 10.000 km² on the North and Central Coast), whereas dense cloud-forest canopy, acid tropical soils and steep terrain limit recovery across the Eastern Montaña and Yungas Slopes (0,05 sites per 10.000 km²) [@nystrom2010chachapoya]. Sub-regional population totals therefore rely on ecological carrying-capacity calibration rather than proportional site scaling.

Third, converting monumental site footprints into resident urban headcounts carries substantial uncertainty at multi-functional ceremonial hubs. At Cahuachi, Chavín de Huántar and Caral, large plazas and platform mounds served periodic regional gatherings whose transient pilgrimage numbers far exceeded permanent resident households [@silverman2009cahuachi; @turner1999geological; @solis2001dating]. Conversely, radiocarbon marine reservoir offsets along the upwelling Humboldt littoral require careful isotopic adjustment when comparing coastal shell-midden dates against highland terrestrial samples [@vaughn2014about; @eerkens2024long].

Fourth, our 1438AD closing horizon represents a political and analytical boundary rather than a demographic discontinuity. Several Late Intermediate capitals - notably Chan Chan, Pachacamac, La Centinela, Quito Pre-Inca and Qosqo Killke - continued growing or underwent imperial restructuring after Pachacuti's expansion into Tawantinsuyu, which is traced separately from 1438AD to 1532AD in the succeeding chapter.

# Conclusion

Across eleven and a half millennia from 10000BC to 1438AD, the Central Andes underwent one of the world's steepest independent trajectories of indigenous demographic growth, expanding 250-fold from 28,8k scattered foragers to 7,2M farmers, herders, artisans and urban dwellers. That expansion rested on two complementary ecological engines: gravity-fed irrigation networks cutting across hyper-arid Pacific river deltas, and vertical agro-pastoral complementarity linking maize valleys, high-altitude tuber terraces, raised lakeside fields and camelid puna pastures [@huckleberry2003geoarchaeological; @stanish2003evolution; @albeck2019produccion].

By 1438AD, population density reached 8,48 inhabitants per km² on the North and Central Coast, 8,47 in the Central Sierra, 7,28 on the South Coast, 4,31 in the Equatorial Sierra and Guayas and 2,74 across the Titicaca-Poopó Altiplano, leaving 92,4% of all Central Andean people concentrated along the coast and highland spine. Whether measured through the archaic pyramids of Caral, the urban artisan quarters of Huacas de Moche and Chan Chan, the orthogonal provincial grids of Wari, the lakeside raised fields of Tiwanaku or the cloud-forest citadels of Chachapoyas and Upano, this 7,2M-strong demographic base formed the human infrastructure that Tawantinsuyu would shortly unify into the largest indigenous empire of the Americas.

# Appendix

## National Distribution of Catalogued Sites

Table \ref{tab:country-sites} aggregates the `r viscount_fmt_number(n_sites, 0L)` catalogued pre-Columbian habitation locales across Peru, Ecuador and Bolivia, pairing national site totals with their gazetteer shares.

```{r tab-country-sites, results='asis'}
c_counts <- unlist(summary_data$settlements_by_country)
c_ord <- sort(c_counts, decreasing = TRUE)
c_df <- data.frame(
  Country = names(c_ord),
  Sites = vapply(as.integer(c_ord), function(v) viscount_fmt_number(v, 0L), character(1)),
  Share = vapply(100 * as.integer(c_ord) / n_sites, function(v) paste0(viscount_fmt_number(v, 1L), "%"), character(1)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
rownames(c_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  c_df,
  "Distribution of 109 catalogued pre-Columbian settlements across modern national territories in the Central Andes.",
  c("Country", "Catalogued Sites", "Share of Gazetteer"),
  list(label = "tab:country-sites", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

## Full Twenty-One Benchmark Series (10000BC to 1438AD)

Table \ref{tab:benchmark-series} documents the full 21-point chronological population series across the 2.230.562,2 km² Central Andean domain alongside aggregate density per km² and inter-benchmark compound annual growth rates.

```{r tab-benchmark-series, results='asis'}
dt <- summary_data$domain_totals
yr_keys <- as.character(sort(as.integer(names(dt))))
fmt_era <- function(y) {
  yi <- as.integer(y)
  if (yi < 0) paste0(abs(yi), "BC") else paste0(yi, "AD")
}
vals <- vapply(yr_keys, function(k) as.numeric(dt[[k]]), numeric(1))
yrs_num <- as.integer(yr_keys)
cagr_str <- vapply(seq_along(yrs_num), function(i) {
  if (i == 1L) return("-")
  dt_y <- yrs_num[i] - yrs_num[i - 1L]
  r_val <- ((vals[i] / vals[i - 1L])^(1 / dt_y) - 1) * 100
  paste0(viscount_fmt_number(r_val, 3L), "%")
}, character(1))

df_series <- data.frame(
  Year = vapply(yr_keys, fmt_era, character(1)),
  Population = vapply(vals, viscount_fmt_pop, character(1)),
  RawPop = vapply(vals, function(v) viscount_fmt_number(v, 0L), character(1)),
  Density = vapply(vals / tot_area, function(d) viscount_fmt_number(d, 3L), character(1)),
  CAGR = cagr_str,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
rownames(df_series) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  df_series,
  "Central Andean domain population series, mean areal density and inter-benchmark compound annual growth rate across 21 benchmarks, 10000BC to 1438AD.",
  c("Benchmark", "Population", "Exact Count", "Density (per km²)", "Interval CAGR"),
  list(label = "tab:benchmark-series", font_size = "scriptsize", max_rows_per_page = 25L)
)
```
